title: Differential improvement in patient-reported outcomes measurement information system (PROMIS) domains after ventriculoperitoneal shunting (VPS) for idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH).
abstract: Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) is a patient-reported outcome tool to overview various functional domains of health. We describe longitudinal changes in various PROMIS domains after ventriculoperitoneal shunting (VPS) for patients with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH).Patients with "probable" iNPH who underwent VPS from December 2017 to January 2025 and had completed pre- and post-operative PROMIS computerized adaptive testing (CAT) were retrospectively reviewed. Domains assessed included anxiety, depression, fatigue, sleep disturbance, pain interference, social ability, and physical function. Generalized additive mixed models (GAMM) were utilized to assess longitudinal changes in each domain while controlling for variable follow-up time and patient-specific repeated measures. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed to identify patterns of change.A total of 173 patients with 461 PROMIS assessments (median 3 per patient) were included with median follow-up time of 10.3 months (IQR 3.3-13.1). Patients undergoing VPS for iNPH had statistically worse pre-operative PROMIS measures (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.05) in all domains except sleep disturbance. Overall, statistically significant and temporally durable T-score improvements after VPS were identified in fatigue, physical function, and social ability. Differential patterns of post-VPS PROMIS changes disclosed three distinct patient clusters with differing baseline PROMIS functions and comorbidity burdens.Approximately half of iNPH patients report significant improvement in various PROMIS domains longitudinally after VPS. Physical function demonstrated both the greatest magnitude of baseline dysfunction and improvement after VPS. With additional notable improvements in fatigue, and social ability, VPS may improve multiple functional healthcare-related quality of life domains.© 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined how a surgical procedure called ventriculoperitoneal shunting, which drains excess fluid from around the brain to treat a condition called idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, affects patients' quality of life and daily functioning. The study looked back at 173 patients who had this surgery between 2017 and 2025 and completed quality of life surveys before and after their operation, with most patients completing multiple surveys over about ten months. The results showed that patients had significant improvements in three main areas after surgery: tiredness levels, physical ability to move and function, and social interactions, while improvements in other areas like anxiety and depression were less consistent. About half of the patients reported meaningful improvements in various aspects of their quality of life after the surgery, with physical function showing the biggest improvement from the worst starting point. These findings suggest that this surgical procedure can help multiple areas of patients' lives, though doctors should recognize that different patients may experience different patterns of improvement based on their individual circumstances and other health conditions.

title: Sotatercept Improves Right Heart Mechanics Despite Reduced Myocardial Contractility in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: A Prospective Exercise Hemodynamic Study.
abstract: The right ventricular (RV) response to pressure overload is a crucial determinant of outcomes in pulmonary arterial (PA) hypertension. Sotatercept improves clinical outcomes, but its effects on the right ventricle have been inconsistent. We evaluated the effects of sotatercept on load-independent measures of RV contractility, RV-PA coupling, and right heart deformation at rest and exertion in patients with PA hypertension.In this prospective trial among participants with PA hypertension recruited between July 2024 and May 2025, we performed simultaneous echocardiography and invasive pressure measurements during rest and exercise to evaluate changes in RV contractility (end-systolic elastance [Ees]), afterload (PA elastance [Ea]), RV-PA coupling (ratio of arterial Ea to Ees), and right heart deformation, including RV and right atrial strain, before and after 24 weeks of sotatercept using mixed models.Among 30 participants (n=21; 70% female; mean age, 49.3 years [SD 13.5]), sotatercept decreased PA Ea. These changes were associated with reduced RV contractility, PA pulsatility index, and the maximal rate of RV pressure increase over time (dP/dtmax; P<0.001 for all). The decrease in Ees was associated with a decrease in PA Ea (r=+0.70 [95% CI, +0.44 to +0.85]; P<0.0001) with preserved RV-PA coupling (mean difference, +0.08 [95% CI, -0.11 to +0.26]; P=0.42). Although systolic indices measured at the base of the right ventricle (tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion and systolic velocity of the lateral tricuspid annulus) decreased after sotatercept use, there was an increase in RV free wall-dependent systolic indices, including resting and exercise RV free wall strain (mean difference, +6.2% [95% CI, +4.5 to +7.8]; P<0.0001) and fractional area change (P=0.0001). Beyond the right ventricle, there was also improved right atrial filling and contractile performance across rest and exercise (P<0.0001 for all).Sotatercept decreases RV contractility in proportion to reduced afterload, while preserving the RV-PA coupling relationship. Despite decreased RV contractility, global measures of right heart performance, such as RV free wall strain and RA strain, improve, alongside redistribution of RV deformation from annular motion to free wall shortening. These data suggest that sotatercept causes an energetically favorable reduction in resting RV contractility to match the lower afterload, which does not appear physiologically detrimental when considering the concurrent improvement in RV free wall contractile mechanics and exertional right heart reserve.URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT06409026.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how a drug called sotatercept affects the right side of the heart in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension, a serious condition where blood vessels in the lungs become stiff and narrow. In this study, thirty patients received sotatercept for twenty-four weeks while doctors measured their heart function using ultrasound and pressure monitoring both at rest and during exercise. The drug reduced the workload on the right ventricle, the chamber that pumps blood to the lungs, and surprisingly the heart responded by decreasing its own pumping strength in a balanced way that kept the heart functioning efficiently. Although some measurements at the base of the right ventricle decreased, the overall performance of the heart muscle improved, particularly in how well the free wall of the right ventricle contracted and how well the right atrium filled with blood. These findings suggest that sotatercept helps the heart work more efficiently by reducing unnecessary strain, which could explain why the drug improves patient outcomes even though it lowers the heart's raw contractile force.

title: Real-World Experience With the Extravascular Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator Through 1 Year: The Enlighten Post Approval Registry Study.
abstract: The extravascular implantable cardioverter defibrillator (EV-ICD) was developed to provide defibrillation and antitachycardia pacing therapy without the need for intravascular lead placement. Premarket clinical trials reported EV-ICD safety and efficacy through 3 years, but a real-world assessment of the Aurora EV-ICD system, which includes a novel sensing discriminator, is needed. The objective of this analysis was to assess real-world therapy efficacy and safety of the EV-ICD through 1 year.Enlighten: The EV-ICD Post Approval Registry is a prospective, global, real-world registry that included patients who underwent an EV-ICD implantation attempt. The main safety analysis was freedom from all system- or procedure-related major complications through 1 year. Event rates at 1 year were calculated using the Kaplan-Meier method.EV-ICD system implantation was attempted by 168 implanters in 787 patients (49.1±15.2 years old; 28.7% women; 34.1% secondary prevention). Tunneling and lead placement in the substernal space were achieved in 781 of 787 patients (99.2%), with 758 patients (96.3%) remaining implanted following defibrillation and electrical testing. One-year freedom from major system- or procedure-related complications was 89.1% (95% CI, 86.3%-91.3%). The 1-year rate of first appropriate therapy (shock, antitachycardia pacing, or both) was 7.3% (95% CI, 5.5-9.6). Shock success for discrete spontaneous episodes was 100% (61 of 61), and the generalized estimating equations antitachycardia pacing success rate, to account for multiple episodes per patient, was 74.2% for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. The 1-year rate of first inappropriate shock was 7.1% (95% CI, 5.4-9.4), with noncardiac oversensing as the main cause (40.5% of inappropriately shocked episodes).In the largest prospective worldwide cohort of patients with an EV-ICD to date, both antitachycardia pacing and shock therapy were effective, while the rate of major complications agreed with the premarket experience through 1 year. These data demonstrate that positive outcomes of the EV-ICD are retained in everyday clinical practice in a large, global cohort with an expanded number of implanters.URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT06048731.

llm_summary: Researchers examined a new type of heart device called an extravascular implantable cardioverter defibrillator, or EV-ICD, which can treat dangerous heart rhythms without requiring wires to be placed inside blood vessels like traditional devices do. In this real-world study, nearly 800 patients from around the world received the EV-ICD implant, and doctors tracked how well the device worked and how safe it was over one year of follow-up. The results showed that the device successfully delivered therapy when needed, with shock treatment working perfectly in all cases and pacing therapy working about 74 percent of the time for a specific type of abnormal heart rhythm. The major complication rate of about 11 percent matched what doctors had seen in earlier testing, meaning the device performed as expected when used by many different doctors in everyday practice rather than just in controlled research settings. These findings suggest that the EV-ICD is a reliable option for patients who need protection from life-threatening heart rhythms and may be especially valuable for those who cannot tolerate traditional devices with internal wires.

title: Hemodynamic Flow Signatures: A Novel Paradigm for the Evaluation of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Performance.
abstract: A new paradigm for understanding transcatheter aortic valve (TAV) success is emerging, which hinges on whether a device reinstates physiological aortic flow. Limitations of echocardiography prevent complex flow assessment. Meanwhile, 4-dimensional flow cardiac magnetic resonance offers superior quantification of time-resolved 3-dimensional flow dynamics, permitting assessment of systolic flow displacement (reflecting eccentricity), systolic flow reversal ratio (reflecting conduit inefficiency), wall shear stress, and energetic efficiency. Abnormal aortic flow can persist after TAV replacement, despite reduction in transvalvular gradient. Persistent nonphysiological flow is thought to increase energy losses, reduce left ventricular ejection efficiency, and impair optimal afterload reduction, which theoretically may limit left ventricular reverse remodeling. Restoration of near-normal flow is a plausible therapeutic target for evaluating TAV performance. However, whether physiological flow restoration post-TAV replacement may enhance left ventricular mass reduction, increase TAV durability, and improve patient-relevant outcomes is unknown, and further research is crucial. Future clinical translation of cardiac magnetic resonance flow metrics also depends on automated extraction of systolic flow displacement and systolic flow reversal ratio, and postprocessing standardization. This review provides a perspective on 4-dimensional flow cardiac magnetic resonance for evaluating aortic flow post-TAV replacement, which may have the potential to refine TAV platform selection, inform next-generation device design, and hypothetically predict left ventricular recovery.

llm_summary: Researchers examined a new way to evaluate how well artificial heart valves work by looking at blood flow patterns rather than just measuring pressure differences across the valve. The study used advanced heart imaging called four-dimensional flow cardiac magnetic resonance, which creates detailed pictures of how blood moves through the aorta (the main artery leaving the heart) over time, allowing doctors to measure things like flow direction, efficiency, and energy loss. The research found that even when artificial valves successfully reduce pressure buildup, abnormal blood flow patterns can persist and may cause the heart to work less efficiently and prevent the heart muscle from shrinking back to normal size. If future studies prove that restoring normal blood flow patterns after valve replacement helps the heart recover better and makes the artificial valves last longer, this could change how doctors choose which valve to use for each patient and guide the design of better devices. The main challenge moving forward is developing automated computer tools to measure these flow patterns consistently and conducting larger studies to confirm whether fixing blood flow patterns actually improves patient outcomes and heart function.

title: Sustained proton-pump inhibitor exposure and incident age-related macular degeneration: a new-user, population-based cohort study.
abstract: Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) may disrupt lysosomal acidification, a pathway implicated in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) pathogenesis. We evaluated whether sustained PPI exposure increased the risk of incident AMD in older adults aged ≥60 years.This retrospective observational cohort study included adults aged ≥60 years with sustained PPI exposure, matched 1:1 to unexposed controls on demographics, overall health, healthcare utilisation, cardiometabolic factors. Participants were identified from electronic health records. Sustained PPI exposure was defined as ≥2 years of cumulative use within 3 years of the first prescription. Fine-Gray models treating death as a competing event estimated subdistribution hazard ratios (sHRs) for AMD within 10 years; cause-specific Cox models provided complementary HRs. Analyses included histamine H2-receptor antagonists (H2-antagonists) as a negative exposure control and active comparator.Incident AMD occurred in 814/49 796 PPI exposed participants (1.64%) and 668/49 796 controls (1.34%) (overall sHR=1.24, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.38; p<0.001; HR=1.25, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.38, p<0.001). Proportional sHRs were non-constant; sHRs were 1.09 (95% CI 0.91 to 1.29) before 2.5 years and 1.33 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.51) thereafter. For non-exudative AMD, 640 PPI exposed (1.29%) and 510 unexposed (1.02%) participants developed disease (overall sHR=1.28, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.44; p<0.001, HR=1.29, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.44, p<0.001). Among those with non-exudative AMD, 190/2503 PPI-exposed participants (7.59%) and 179/2503 controls (7.15%) progressed to exudative AMD (sHR and HR=1.03, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.26; p=0.802 and p=0.801, respectively). No association was observed between H2-antagonists and AMD (sHR=1.02, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.19; p=0.784; HR=1.03, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.20, p=0.729). Results were consistent in the active-comparator analysis (reciprocal overall sHR=1.24, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.48; p=0.016; HR=1.25, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.49, p=0.012).Sustained PPI exposure was associated with a modestly higher AMD risk, whereas no association was observed with H2-antagonists. The consistency of the active-comparator findings supports the potential specificity of this association and warrants further investigation to determine its clinical implications.© Author(s) (or their employer(s)) 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a common stomach medication called proton-pump inhibitors, which reduce acid production in the stomach, might increase the risk of age-related macular degeneration, a disease that damages the central part of the eye and causes vision loss in older adults. The study followed nearly 50,000 people aged 60 and older who took these medications for at least two years and compared them to a similar group who did not take the medication, tracking whether they developed eye disease over ten years. People who took proton-pump inhibitors had a slightly higher rate of developing age-related macular degeneration compared to those who did not take the medication, with the increased risk becoming more noticeable after two and a half years of use. The findings suggest that long-term use of this common medication may have a modest effect on eye health, though the researchers note that other stomach medications called H2-antagonists did not show this same association, which supports that the effect is specific to proton-pump inhibitors. Further research is needed to understand whether this connection is truly caused by the medication and to determine what this means for patients who need to take these drugs for their stomach problems.

Artificial intelligence technology can now analyze detailed three-dimensional images of these plaques to identify dangerous features that tend to appear in the section of the vessel just before the area of greatest narrowing.

title: Measuring Symptom Severity and Health-Related Quality-of-Life with Hemorrhoid Treatments: Systematic Review.
abstract: Hemorrhoids are common and relief anchors on symptom improvement. Despite several available treatment options, the optimal patient-reported outcome measure for contemporary clinical trials is not established.We aimed to systematically assess patient-reported outcome measures that measure hemorrhoid symptom severity and/or health-related quality of life.A systematic review was performed using PubMed and Embase (1980-2025).Prospective development/validation studies evaluating patient-reported outcome measures relevant to hemorrhoidal disease.Patient-reported outcome measures were evaluated on key measurement properties of reliability, internal consistency, construct validity, and responsiveness according to COSMIN v2.0 criteria.Of the 1,266 total studies reviewed, nine patient-reported outcome measures were identified: seven measure symptom severity and six measure health-related quality-of-life. Three demonstrated reliability, internal consistency, construct validity, and responsiveness. The Patient Reported Outcome Measure-Haemorrhoidal Impact And Satisfaction Score comprehensively measures symptom severity, health-related quality-of-life, and treatment satisfaction. The Hemorrhoidal Disease Symptom Score classifies patients with high or low symptom load, and when used in combination with Short Health Scale-Hemorrhoidal Disease, also measures impact on health-related quality of life.Preference toward specific measures may differ between clinical trials and clinical practice.We identify two viable patient-reported outcome measures for use in future clinical trials that evaluate hemorrhoid interventions.Copyright © The ASCRS 2026.

llm_summary: Hemorrhoids are a common health problem, and doctors need reliable ways to measure how well treatments work by asking patients about their symptoms and quality of life. Researchers searched through thousands of medical studies published between 1980 and 2025 to find and evaluate different questionnaires and measurement tools that patients use to report how severe their hemorrhoid symptoms are and how much the condition affects their daily life. Out of nine different measurement tools they found, only three were shown to be reliable, consistent, and actually able to detect when patients improved after treatment. The researchers identified two specific tools as the best options for future medical trials testing new hemorrhoid treatments: one called the Patient Reported Outcome Measure-Haemorrhoidal Impact And Satisfaction Score that measures symptoms, quality of life, and satisfaction all together, and another called the Hemorrhoidal Disease Symptom Score that can be combined with another tool to measure both symptom severity and life impact. These findings will help doctors and researchers choose the right measurement tools when testing whether new hemorrhoid treatments actually work and improve patients' lives.

title: MRI assessment of extramural venous invasion in rectal cancer: a practical pictorial review.
abstract: Extramural venous invasion (EMVI), the spread of rectal tumor cells into veins beyond the muscularis propria, is one of the most prognostically powerful preoperative findings detectable on pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Meta-analytic evidence indicates that baseline mrEMVI is associated with an approximately fourfold increased risk of metachronous metastases (OR 3.91; 95% CI 2.61-5.86), and it independently predicts inferior disease-free and overall survival. Despite this evidence, MRI-based EMVI assessment remains inconsistently applied in routine practice. This pictorial review provides a structured, image-focused approach to MRI-detected EMVI, covering the technical requirements for reliable detection, relevant venous anatomy, imaging hallmarks on high-resolution T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted imaging, the validated five-point grading scale, the most clinically significant mimics and pitfalls, and the specific challenges of restaging after neoadjuvant therapy. We also summarize the clinical implications of EMVI grading for treatment intensification, lateral lymph node management, and organ-preservation decisions. Graded MRI assessment of EMVI provides clinically meaningful prognostic information beyond binary positive/negative reporting and is increasingly used to inform multidisciplinary decisions in rectal cancer, although evidence that grade-directed treatment modification improves outcomes remains limited. Reproducible interpretation requires attention to key pitfalls, including equivocal grade 2 findings, small-caliber vessels, and reduced diagnostic reliability after neoadjuvant therapy.© 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined how doctors can better detect a serious condition in rectal cancer where tumor cells spread into blood vessels beyond the muscle layer of the bowel, which is one of the strongest predictors of whether cancer will return in other parts of the body. The study is a pictorial review, meaning the authors used images and detailed explanations to teach doctors how to properly identify this condition using MRI scans, which is a type of imaging test that takes detailed pictures inside the body. The review found that patients with this venous invasion condition have about four times higher risk of developing cancer in distant parts of their body and have worse survival rates, yet many doctors do not consistently look for or report this finding in their routine practice. The authors provided a structured guide covering the technical requirements for accurate detection, the specific appearance of the condition on MRI images, a five-point grading scale to measure severity, and common mistakes that can lead to misdiagnosis. While graded assessment of this condition provides valuable information to help doctors make treatment decisions and determine which patients need more aggressive therapy, doctors still need more research to prove that changing treatment based on these grades actually improves patient outcomes.

title: Identifying the trajectory of SPPADE symptoms in patients with cancer using electronic health record data.
abstract: The longitudinal course (trajectory) of symptoms in patients with cancer has been understudied. Sleep disturbance, pain, physical function impairment, anxiety, depression, and energy deficit/fatigue (SPPADE) are particularly common in patients with cancer. This study characterizes the trajectory patterns of SPPADE symptoms in a large and diverse sample of patients with cancer and identifies factors associated with distinct trajectories.To identify the optimal number and functional forms of the symptom trajectories, latent class growth analysis was conducted. Electronic health record (EHR) data were analyzed from 14,590 patients in the Enhanced EHR-facilitated Cancer Symptom Control (E2C2) trial cohort with at least 3 symptom assessments within a 12-month period. Each SPPADE symptom was rated on a 0-10 numeric rating scale. Multivariable multinomial logistic regression was used to determine factors associated with membership in the symptom trajectory subgroups.Four distinct trajectory patterns were similar across symptoms. The average sample distribution of membership in a trajectory class across the 6 symptoms was 65.5% for low severity stable, 15.5% for high severity stable, 10.7% for improving, and 8.4% for worsening. Being employed, married/partnered, better educated, older, and not having metastatic disease were independently associated with membership in the low stable trajectory of SPPADE symptoms. Cancer site generally did not influence symptom trajectory class membership.For oncology practices that routinely use patient-reported outcomes to assess symptoms, EHR data can be a source for characterizing symptom trajectories. Knowledge of factors associated with trajectory class membership could be useful in clinical research and for tailoring evidence-based symptom management strategies.© 2026. The Author(s).

llm_summary: Researchers examined how common cancer-related symptoms like sleep problems, pain, fatigue, anxiety, and depression change over time in patients, since doctors have not studied these symptom patterns thoroughly before. The study analyzed health records from over 14,500 cancer patients who reported their symptom levels multiple times over a year, using a statistical method to identify different patterns of how symptoms progressed. The researchers found four main patterns that were similar across all the symptoms studied: about two-thirds of patients had low and stable symptoms, roughly one-sixth had high but stable symptoms, about one-tenth improved over time, and a small group of about eight percent got worse. Patients who were employed, married, better educated, older, and did not have cancer that had spread to other parts of their body were more likely to experience low and stable symptoms. These findings suggest that doctors can use patient symptom records already stored in electronic health systems to identify which patients need extra help managing their symptoms and to develop better treatment plans tailored to each patient's needs.

title: Projected Benefit of Bilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy by Age in BRCA Carriers.
abstract: Women with a BRCA1 or BRCA2 variant face a high lifetime risk of ovarian cancer and are often advised to undergo preventive surgery (bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy [BSO]) before cancer develops. The recommended age of BSO is 35 years for BRCA1 carriers and is 45 years for BRCA2 carriers, but some women choose to delay surgery until the age of menopause; there is no standard upper age at which surgery is no longer advised.To estimate the residual lifetime risk of ovarian cancer among BRCA carriers by current age and projected age at BSO.This was a prospective cohort study in an international cohort of BRCA carriers monitored for incident ovarian cancer. A life table analysis used age-specific ovarian cancer incidence rates and competing mortality rates to estimate lifetime risk of ovarian cancer among women with a BRCA1 or BRCA2 pathogenic variant with both ovaries intact and no prior ovarian cancer at baseline. Patients were recruited between 1995 and 2024 across 24 international centers, and the mean (SD) follow-up was 4.4 (3.9) years.Timing of BSO, defined as immediate BSO, delayed BSO, or no BSO.Residual lifetime risk of ovarian cancer.The cohort consisted of 4286 BRCA1 and 1427 BRCA2 carriers between the ages of 30 and 74 years at baseline (mean [SD] age, 42.0 [10.8] years). There were 249 incident ovarian cancers in the follow-up period. The lifetime risk of ovarian cancer was 55.0% (95% CI, 48.8-61.9) for a BRCA1 carrier and 24.1% (95% CI, 15.1-36.6) for a BRCA2 carrier. A 30-year-old BRCA1 carrier with BSO delayed to age 50 years had a projected residual ovarian cancer risk of 23.9% (95% CI, 20.7-27.4). At age 75 years, the residual risk of ovarian cancer was estimated to be 8.4% (95% CI, 1.7-22.7) for a BRCA1 carrier and 3.7% (95% CI, 0.1-22.7) for a BRCA2 carrier.The residual risk of ovarian cancer for older women in good health is sufficiently high to consider preventive surgery. BRCA1 carriers who defer BSO until age 50 years may face a substantial risk of developing ovarian cancer.

llm_summary: Women who carry mutations in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes have a significantly higher risk of developing ovarian cancer during their lifetime, which is why doctors often recommend surgical removal of the ovaries and fallopian tubes as a preventive measure. Researchers examined data from nearly 5,700 women with these genetic mutations across 24 international medical centers over an average of four years to determine how the timing of preventive surgery affects the remaining risk of ovarian cancer. The study found that women with BRCA1 mutations face a 55 percent lifetime risk of ovarian cancer, while those with BRCA2 mutations face a 24 percent risk, and delaying surgery until age 50 still leaves a substantial 24 percent risk for younger BRCA1 carriers. Even older women in their seventies who have not had the surgery removed still face meaningful risks of developing ovarian cancer, suggesting that preventive surgery may be beneficial across a wider age range than currently recommended. These findings suggest that doctors should reconsider their current age guidelines for recommending preventive surgery and may need to offer this option to older women who remain in good health.

title: Intraoperative Ketamine and Chronic Opioid Use After Lumbar Spine Surgery in Patients With and Without Opioid-Use Disorder: A Retrospective Database Analysis.
abstract: Persistent opioid use after lumbar spine surgery (LSS) remains a major clinical concern. Ketamine is frequently included in multimodal perioperative analgesic regimens for its attenuating effects on central sensitization and its potential to reduce acute postoperative pain and opioid requirements. However, evidence regarding whether intraoperative ketamine influences longer-term outpatient postoperative opioid use is limited and mixed. We aimed to evaluate whether intraoperative ketamine administration is associated with differences in chronic postoperative opioid use after LSS, stratified by preoperative opioid exposure status.We performed a propensity-matched retrospective cohort study using the U.S. based TriNetX Global Research Network-a database containing de-identified electronic health records-including adult patients who underwent LSS between January 2010 and December 2024. Patients were grouped based on receipt of an intraoperative ketamine and stratified by preoperative opioid status (opioid-naive or with opioid-use disorder [OUD]). Propensity score matching was used to balance demographic characteristics and relevant comorbidities. The primary outcome was the presence of outpatient opioid prescriptions at 48 hours, 6 weeks, 3, 6, and 12 months after surgery. Secondary outcomes included opioid-related adverse events and new diagnosis of OUD within 12 months of surgery.After matching, 53,639 opioid-naive patients and 2031 patients with OUD were analyzed. In opioid-naive patients, intraoperative ketamine exposure was associated with higher rates of outpatient opioid prescribing in the early postoperative period at 48 hours (P < .001; risk ratio [RR] 1.23; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.22-1.25) and 6 weeks (P < .001; RR 1.14; 95% CI, 1.10-1.18), whereas no meaningful differences were observed at 3, 6, or 12 months. In patients with OUD, ketamine exposure was associated with higher rates of opioid prescribing only through 48 hours postoperatively. Opioid-related adverse events and new OUD diagnoses were not reduced but were, in fact, similar or more frequent among ketamine-exposed patients.In this large, real-world cohort, intraoperative ketamine was not associated with lower rates of chronic opioid dispensing after LSS in either opioid-naive or patients with OUD. These database findings reflect the absence of a detectable population-level opioid-sparing signal, and do not exclude dose- or protocol-dependent effects.Copyright © 2026 International Anesthesia Research Society.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether ketamine, a medication sometimes given during surgery to help manage pain, could reduce the need for opioid painkillers (strong narcotic drugs) after lumbar spine surgery, which is a common procedure to address lower back problems. They studied a large database of over 55,000 patients who had this surgery between 2010 and 2024, comparing those who received ketamine during their operation to those who did not, and they looked separately at patients who had never used opioids before and those with opioid-use disorder (a condition where people struggle to control their use of these powerful painkillers). The results showed that patients who received ketamine actually received more opioid prescriptions in the first six weeks after surgery, not fewer, and this pattern held true for both groups of patients. The findings suggest that giving ketamine during surgery did not help reduce long-term opioid use or prevent serious opioid-related problems, which goes against the hope that ketamine might help patients avoid becoming dependent on these strong painkillers. The researchers concluded that while this real-world data does not show ketamine helping with opioid reduction, future studies might still.

title: Ivabradine Use and Exercise Capacity Post-Atrial Switch Repair for Transposition of Great Arteries.
abstract: There are few proven therapies for improving exercise capacity in patients with transposition of the great arteries who have undergone an atrial switch repair.The objective of the study was to evaluate the effect of heart rate lowering using ivabradine on exercise capacity and quality of life in this cohort.In this single-center, randomized, double-blind, crossover study, patients were randomized to ivabradine or placebo for 4 weeks then crossover treatment for 4 weeks. A cardiopulmonary stress test and quality of life assessment were performed at baseline then at weeks 4 and 8. Estimates of difference were described using a mixed effects model.A total of 19 patients were eligible and 10 patients completed the study. Compared to placebo, ivabradine treatment was associated with lower heart rate at baseline (65 ± 3 beats/min on ivabradine vs 79 ± 5 beats/min on placebo, difference -14.6 [-24, -5]; P = 0.008) and at peak exercise (131 ± 7 beats/min vs 146 ± 7 beats/min, difference -15.3 [-24, -6]; P = 0.003). Peak oxygen consumption was 20.4 ± 1.2 mL/kg/min on ivabradine vs 19.2 ± 1.2 mL/kg/min on placebo (difference +1.2 [-0.09, 2.6]; P = 0.06). Peak oxygen pulse was higher on ivabradine compared to placebo (12.5 ± 1.2 vs 10.7 ± 1.2 mL/beat, difference +1.7 [0.9, 2.6]; P = 0.002). Visual analog score was 73.5 ± 5.6 on ivabradine vs 62.5 ± 5.6 on placebo (mean difference 11.0 [-1.6, 23.6]; P = 0.08). One patient developed symptomatic bradycardia and one patient experienced phosphenes.Ivabradine use in patients with transposition of the great arteries and atrial switch repair lowered peak heart rate with exercise and was associated with a higher oxygen pulse. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a heart rate-lowering medication called ivabradine could help improve exercise ability in patients who had undergone a special heart surgery called atrial switch repair for a condition where the major blood vessels of the heart are switched at birth. In this carefully controlled study, ten patients took either ivabradine or a placebo (a fake pill) for four weeks, then switched to the other treatment for another four weeks, with exercise tests and quality of life surveys performed at the beginning and end of each period. When taking ivabradine, patients had significantly lower heart rates both at rest and during peak exercise, and they showed improved oxygen efficiency during exercise, though the overall improvement in peak oxygen consumption was not quite statistically significant. These findings suggest that ivabradine may offer a modest benefit for patients with this specific heart condition by reducing heart rate stress during activity and improving how efficiently their hearts use oxygen. However, the study was small with only ten participants completing it, and some patients experienced side effects like abnormal heart rhythms, so larger studies would be needed to confirm whether this treatment should become standard care for these patients.

llm_summary: Background:  Infective endocarditis is a serious infection of the heart's inner lining that can develop when bacteria or other germs enter the bloodstream and settle on the heart valves or tissue. Mural endocarditis, which refers to infection of the heart wall itself rather than just the valves, is a less common form of this disease that requires careful study to understand how it affects adults and what the best treatment approaches might be.

title: Women in U.S. Neurosurgery Residency Programs: Trends, Leadership, and Program-Level Associations.
abstract: Women's representation in neurosurgery residency has increased over the past decade. To our knowledge, this is the first study evaluating program-level characteristics association with variation in the proportion of women residents.Data were collected in 2024 from program websites, AMA FREIDA, and Doximity. Resident gender was manually identified for 1,581 residents across 110 of 118 neurosurgery programs. Associations with women resident representation were analyzed for geographic region, cost of living, compensation, subspecialty offerings, alumni subspecialization, and program research and reputation rankings. Chair and program director gender and full-time paid female faculty analyses were limited by small samples and incomplete public data. Post-hoc sensitivity analyses contextualized limited-data or mismatched-group tests.Women comprised 27% of residents and 7% of chairs and program directors, whereas 13% of full-time paid faculty were female. No program-level characteristic was significantly associated with women resident representation. However, data for many variables were unavailable for up to half of programs, limiting the strength and generalizability of negative findings.Women's representation among U.S. neurosurgery residents has nearly quadrupled since the 7% reported in 1990, enabling meaningful contemporary evaluation of program-level variation in representation. However, the available cross-sectional data identified no associated program characteristics. Prior literature suggests women applicants prioritize other core aspects of neurosurgical training when selecting programs. Parallel growth among women residents and female applicants may reflect early exposure, mentorship, and engagement with visible women role models. Greater trainee representation may translate into greater faculty and leadership representation, enabling future evaluation of workforce, cultural, and patient care outcomes.Copyright © 2026. llm_summary: Women have made significant progress in neurosurgery, a surgical specialty focused on treating brain and nervous system conditions, with their representation among residents nearly quadrupling from just seven percent in 1990 to twenty-seven percent today. Researchers collected information in 2024 from websites and medical databases about 1,581 residents across 110 neurosurgery training programs to identify which program characteristics, such as location, cost of living, salary, and available specialties, might explain why some programs have more women residents than others. The study found that women made up about a quarter of residents but held only seven percent of leadership positions like chair and program director roles, and just thirteen percent of full-time paid faculty positions. Surprisingly, no specific program feature was strongly linked to having more women residents, though the researchers noted that information was missing for many programs, which made it harder to draw firm conclusions. The researchers suggest that women choosing neurosurgery programs may focus more on training quality and finding visible female role models rather than program characteristics, and they recommend tracking how increasing numbers of women residents might eventually lead to more women in leadership and faculty positions.

title: Association of long-term low estimated glomerular filtration rate after living kidney donation with cardiovascular disease and mortality.
abstract: In the general population, eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2 is associated with increased risks of hypertension, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and mortality, and the risk increases as eGFR further decreases. We studied whether late postdonation (>1 year) low eGFR was associated with similar risks. The association of postdonation time-updated eGFR on time to hypertension, CVD, and mortality was assessed using sequential stratification proportional hazard models adjusting for clinical and demographic characteristics. Of 3,375 living kidney donors (LDs), 1775 (52.5%) developed eGFR<60 ml/min1.73m2 at a mean (SD) age of 57.6 (11.8) years and at 13.6 (11.9) years postdonation; 551 (16.3%) developed eGFR<45 ml/min/1.73m2 at a mean age of 65.0 (12.4) and at 19.1 (11.9) years postdonation. For LDs who reached a postdonation eGFR below 45ml/min/1.73m2, additional decrease of eGFR was associated with an increasing risk of CVD (aHR = 1.34, 95% CI 1.02-1.75 per 10 ml/min/1.73m2 lower eGFR) and mortality (aHR = 1.47, 95% CI:1.23-1.77 10 ml/min/1.73m2 lower eGFR). There was no association with development of hypertension. Our findings suggest that the eGFR threshold at which CVD and mortality risk increases is lower in LDs (<45 ml/min/1.73m2) compared with CKD due to chronic disease (<60 ml/min/1.73m2). llm_summary: Researchers examined whether living kidney donors who gave away one of their two kidneys would face increased risks of heart disease and death if their kidney function declined over time, since these risks are well known in people with chronic kidney disease from other causes. The study followed 3,375 living kidney donors for many years after their surgery, measuring their kidney function through a blood test called estimated glomerular filtration rate, which shows how well kidneys are filtering waste. The researchers found that when donors' kidney function dropped below 45 milliliters per minute per 1. 73 square meters of body surface area (a measurement of kidney health), further declines in function were linked to higher risks of heart disease and death, but not to high blood pressure. Importantly, this dangerous threshold of 45 was lower than the threshold of 60 that doctors use to identify kidney disease risk in the general population, suggesting that kidney donors may need different monitoring guidelines than other patients.

title: Housing-Based Socioeconomic Status at Birth and Infant Mortality in a Population-Based Cohort.
abstract: Socioeconomic status (SES) impacts infant mortality risk, yet measuring individual-level SES in large health datasets remains challenging. We evaluated the association between individual-level SES, measured via the HOUsing-based SocioEconomic Status (HOUSES) index, and infant mortality within a population-based cohort.This retrospective cohort study used the Rochester Epidemiology Project (REP) medical records-linkage system to evaluate live births from 2010 to 2021. The primary exposure was individual-level SES at birth, quantified into quartiles (Q1=lowest SES, Q4=highest SES) using the HOUSES index, which is derived from real property tax assessor data. The primary outcome was infant mortality (death <365 days). Survival probabilities across HOUSES quartiles during the initial 365 days post-birth were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier curves and log-rank tests. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) for infant mortality.Among 79,444 infants with HOUSES data, overall infant mortality was 0.42% (n=332). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated significantly lower survival probability across lower HOUSES quartiles (log-rank p, 0.011). After adjusting for prematurity and congenital anomalies, infants in the lowest HOUSES quartile (Q1) experienced a significantly increased risk of mortality compared to those in the highest quartile (Q4; reference group) (aHR: 1.41; 95% CI: 1.03-1.92; p, 0.031).Lower housing-based SES at birth is independently associated with an increased risk of infant mortality. The HOUSES index represents an objective, scalable tool to identify at-risk families and address social drivers of health in clinical and epidemiological research.Copyright © 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined whether a family's housing situation at the time of a baby's birth could predict the risk of infant death, since poverty and low income are known to affect babies' health outcomes but are difficult to measure accurately in large medical databases. The study looked at nearly eighty thousand babies born between 2010 and 2021 in Rochester, Minnesota, using a tool called the HOUSES index that estimates a family's wealth based on their home's property tax value instead of asking families directly about their income. Babies born into families with the lowest housing-based wealth had a forty-one percent higher risk of dying before their first birthday compared to babies born into the wealthiest families, even after accounting for premature birth and birth defects. This finding shows that housing-based socioeconomic status is an independent risk factor for infant mortality, meaning it matters on its own beyond other medical complications. The HOUSES index could be a useful tool for hospitals and public health programs to identify families who need extra support and resources to help keep their babies healthy.

title: Novel human neutralizing monoclonal antibodies against Pregnancy-Associated Plasma Protein A for the treatment of Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease.
abstract: Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPPA) cleaves insulin-like growth factor (IGF) binding proteins (IGFBP) 2, 4, 5, releasing IGF1. PAPPA is overexpressed in polycystic kidneys and its genetic elimination or suppression by mouse Ansh Labs PAPPA-mAb, which blocks IGFBP4 but not IGFBP5 cleavage, ameliorates polycystic kidney disease (PKD) in Pkd1RC/RC mice. Here, we sought to generate human pan-selective PAPPA-mAbs and test their efficacy in models of advanced and early PKD, using a wide range of doses in mice.Yeast-based expression platforms were used to generate mAbs neutralizing PAPPA-mediated cleavage of IGFBP2, 4, 5 in human epithelial cells (IGF1-induced Akt phosphorylation or ELISAs of full length and PAPPA cleaved C-terminal IGFBP4 fragments as readouts). Hydrogen deuterium exchange (HDX) and cryo-EM were used to map PAPPA and mAb interacting sites. PAPPA-mAb1 (15 or 50 mg/kg/week) and -mAb2 (1, 5 or 50 mg/kg/week) were administered intraperitoneally to male jck mice with advanced PKD from six to 12 weeks; PAPPA-mAb2 (0.3, 3 or 30 mg/kg/week) was administered to male and female Pkd1RC/RC mice with early PKD from four to 16 weeks of age.PAPPA-mAb1 and -mAb2 blocked PAPPA mediated cleavage of IGFBP2, 4, 5. HDX and cryo-EM identified PAPPA regions interacting with IGFBP2, 4, 5 protected by both PAPPA-mAbs. All doses administered to male mice equally demonstrated excellent target engagement and ameliorated cystic disease, inflammation, fibrosis, and inhibited IGF1Rβ and downstream signaling. PAPPA-mAb2 protected female less than male Pkd1RC/RC mice. Both mAbs compared favorably to Ansh Labs mAb in cell systems and in vivo.Our study confirms that PAPPA-mAbs are a promising new targeted therapy for autosomal dominant PKD. Excellent target engagement and low dose effectiveness of novel human PAPPA-mAbs, with implications for long-term safety, and sexual dimorphism of the therapeutic response should be considered in the design of clinical trials.Copyright © 2026. llm_summary: Researchers examined a protein called PAPPA that becomes overactive in polycystic kidney disease, a genetic disorder where cysts gradually destroy kidney function, to see if blocking it could slow the disease. The team created new antibodies, which are immune proteins that can target and neutralize harmful substances, designed to block PAPPA's ability to break down other proteins that control cell growth in the kidneys. When they tested these antibodies in mice with advanced and early stages of polycystic kidney disease at various doses, they found that the antibodies successfully reduced cyst formation, inflammation, and scarring while blocking the growth signals that drive the disease. The results suggest that these new antibodies could become an effective treatment for polycystic kidney disease, especially since they worked well even at low doses, which is important for long-term safety in patients. The researchers noted that the treatment worked better in male mice than female mice, which means future human trials will need to carefully consider how sex differences might affect the therapy's effectiveness.

title: What makes support groups effective and sustainable? an exploratory qualitative study of people living with HIV in the ICON-3 practice-based research network, Nigeria.
abstract: To explore how people living with HIV (PLHIV) perceive the factors that influence the effectiveness and long-term sustainability of HIV support groups in Nigeria.Exploratory qualitative study using semi-structured focus group discussions (FGDs).Twelve health facilities across Nigeria's six geopolitical zones, representing diverse urban and rural contexts affiliated with the Nigeria Implementation Science Alliance and ICON 3 Practice-Based Research Network (ICON-3 PBRN).110 PLHIV, including support group members and leaders, participated in 12 FGDs. Participants were recruited purposively based on experience with support groups and HIV care.FGDs were conducted between March and May 2025, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The psychosocial model of mental health guided inquiry and interpretation.Support groups were perceived as transformative psychosocial and informational spaces that foster belonging, reduce isolation and enhance health literacy and treatment adherence. Key facilitators included vocational skill-building, cooperative income-generating activities and opportunities for economic self-sufficiency. Barriers included stigma and fear of disclosure, financial hardship (especially transport costs and loss of income), leadership instability, weak communication systems, inadequate infrastructure and breaches of confidentiality. Sustainability was linked to improved leadership, livelihood support, community awareness, reliable funding and multi-sectoral partnerships involving NGOs, philanthropists and health facilities.Support groups in Nigeria function as critical psychosocial and economic support systems for PLHIV but remain constrained by structural, economic and stigma-related challenges. Strengthening their sustainability requires integrating psychosocial and livelihood interventions, improving governance structures and developing multisectoral collaborations. llm_summary: Researchers examined what makes HIV support groups work well and last long in Nigeria, where people living with HIV face many challenges in getting care and managing their health. The study involved 110 people with HIV who attended support groups across twelve different health facilities in Nigeria, and researchers held group discussions with them between March and May 2025 to hear their experiences and opinions. People said that support groups were very helpful because they reduced feelings of loneliness, taught them important health information, and helped them stick to their medicines, especially when the groups also offered job training and ways to earn money. The biggest problems stopping these groups from working well were stigma and shame around HIV, lack of money for transportation, unstable leadership, poor communication between members, and sometimes people breaking the privacy rules by sharing others' secrets. To make these support groups stronger and keep them going, the researchers say communities need better leadership, more money for living expenses, awareness campaigns to fight stigma, steady funding, and partnerships between hospitals, charities, and other organizations working together.

title: Predicting Oral Cancer From Precursor Lesions: The Case for a Standardized Framework of Analysis to Improve Prediction Modeling.
abstract: Oral Cancer often occurs from the transformation of precursor lesions, and this offers an opportunity for early detection. Current methods to assess risk of precursor lesion progression to oral cancer incompletely predict risk. A multimodal framework that leverages machine learning is needed to improve prediction. In this manuscript, we propose more standardization in the study of OPMD across sites and propose a framework aligned to the principles of the NCI's Human Tissue Atlas Network (HTAN). We explore whole exome sequencing for genomic risk, methylation array for environmental genetic regulation, RNA sequencing for transcriptional control of cellular programs with spatial transcriptomics to fulfill the spatial requirements of HTAN. Moreover, we propose a machine learning (ML) analysis whereby a learned image-molecular association is created by integrating H&E histology and sequencing results. Once these associations are learned, a "Teacher-Student" model can be created whereby the Student model can be deployed to infer the "molecular associations" from H&E and patient covariates alone. Such a framework integrating multiomic data across multiple different biologic processes and time points can help to better understand and potentially even predict the biologic events that underlie oral cancer initiation.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Oral cancer often develops from precursor lesions, which are abnormal tissue growths that can potentially turn into cancer, making early detection crucial for better patient outcomes. Researchers proposed a new standardized framework that combines multiple types of genetic and molecular testing along with machine learning, which is a computer system that learns patterns from data, to better predict which precursor lesions will develop into cancer. The framework uses several advanced techniques including whole genome sequencing to identify genetic risk factors, methylation testing to understand how environmental factors affect genes, and RNA sequencing to see which genes are active in cells, all combined with detailed tissue images. The researchers suggest creating a special machine learning model that learns to connect tissue appearance with molecular information, and then use this knowledge to predict cancer risk from simple tissue samples and patient information alone. This integrated approach using multiple types of biological data collected over time could help doctors better understand how oral cancer develops and potentially predict which patients are at highest risk before cancer actually forms.

title: Hormone Replacement Therapy and Recurrence Risk in Postmenopausal Idiopathic Subglottic Stenosis.
abstract: To evaluate whether systemic hormone replacement therapy (HRT) influences recurrence outcomes in postmenopausal patients with idiopathic subglottic stenosis (iSGS).Retrospective cohort study.Tertiary academic medical center.Postmenopausal women (≥50 years) with iSGS who underwent laser-wedge excision between 2002 and 2024 were included. Patients were categorized by systemic HRT exposure (oral estrogen, progesterone, combined estrogen-progesterone, or transdermal estrogen) at or before their first surgery. Overdispersion was assessed for all Poisson models; given significant overdispersion, negative binomial regression with a log-offset for follow-up time was used as the primary model. Surgery-free intervals were analyzed using linear mixed models, and time to first recurrence using Cox regression. Models were adjusted for age, body mass index (BMI), parity, oophorectomy, follow-up length, surgery type, and serial intralesional steroid injections (SILSI) use.Among 125 patients, 96 had never used HRT (Never HRT) and 29 used HRT, including 19 actively using HRT at presentation (Current HRT), 5 past users, and 5 subsequent users. The HRT versus Never-HRT recurrence rate comparison was not significant (adjusted incidence rate ratio [IRR] = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.48-1.37, P = .422). However, Current HRT use was associated with a 53% lower adjusted recurrence rate versus Never-HRT use (adjusted IRR = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.25, 0.89, P = .0203). Surgery-free intervals and time to first recurrence trended longer in Current HRT users but were not statistically significant.Current HRT use at presentation was associated with significantly fewer recurrences in postmenopausal iSGS patients. These findings may inform individualized, shared decision-making regarding HRT use in this population.© 2026 American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery Foundation.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether hormone replacement therapy, a treatment that adds hormones back into the body after menopause, might affect how often a throat condition called idiopathic subglottic stenosis returns in postmenopausal women. The study looked back at medical records from 125 women who had laser surgery to treat this narrowing of the airway between 2002 and 2024, comparing those who were actively using hormone replacement therapy at the time of surgery with those who had never used it. Women who were currently using hormone replacement therapy at the time of their surgery had about 53 percent fewer recurrences of the condition compared to women who never used hormone replacement therapy. These findings suggest that hormone replacement therapy might help reduce how often this throat condition comes back after surgery, which could help doctors and patients make better decisions together about whether to use this treatment. More research is needed to confirm these results and understand exactly how hormone replacement therapy might protect against recurrence of this condition.

title: Patterns of care, outcomes, and prognostics for transformed follicular lymphoma in the rituximab era.
abstract: Histologic transformation (HT) is the leading of death in follicular lymphoma (FL), yet outcomes remain poorly defined due to small cohorts and heterogenous definitions. To characterize outcomes and treatment patterns in the rituximab era we analyzed 344 patients with an initial biopsy-confirmed FL diagnosis between 2002 and 2022 who subsequently developed biopsy-confirmed HT in the Lymphoma Epidemiology of Outcomes (LEO) Consortium of Real-World Evidence (CReWE). Median age at HT was 64 (IQR 57-72). Initial treatment for HT (index therapy) included R-CHOP-like (n=154, 45%) and aggressive/salvage (n=85, 25%). The median event free survival (EFS) from HT was 9 months (95% CI, 7-11), and 2-year EFS was 30% (95% CI, 26%-36%). Median OS from HT was 4.9 years (95% CI, 4.0-7.5) with 2-year and 5-year OS estimates of 66% (95% CI, 61%-71%) and 49% (95% CI, 43%-56%), respectively. Relapses after HT occurred in 60%. Relapse histology included DLBCL 70%, FL 15%, and HGBCL 12%. Treatment following relapse from index therapy was commonly aggressive/salvage (often incorporating ASCT/CAR-T) in 44%. llm_summary: Researchers examined a serious complication called histologic transformation, which occurs when slow-growing follicular lymphoma (a type of blood cancer) suddenly becomes aggressive, because this transformation is a leading cause of death in lymphoma patients yet doctors did not have clear information about how patients fare after it happens. The study looked at 344 patients diagnosed with follicular lymphoma between 2002 and 2022 who later developed this transformation, tracking their treatment patterns and survival outcomes using real-world medical records from multiple cancer centers. Most patients received standard chemotherapy combined with a targeted antibody drug called rituximab as their first treatment for the transformed cancer, and while some patients survived longer than five years, many experienced cancer recurrence within two years, with about 60 percent of patients having their cancer return. The findings show that patients who develop this transformation face a challenging prognosis, with roughly one-third of patients remaining cancer-free two years after treatment and half surviving five years or longer. Future research should focus on identifying which patients are at highest risk for transformation and developing better treatment strategies to improve survival for those who experience this serious complication.

title: Clinical outcomes and safety of the immune checkpoint inhibitor rechallenge in Hodgkin lymphoma: an off-trial analysis.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are effective in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), but immune-related adverse events (irAEs) may lead to treatment interruption in some patients. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 145 patients with cHL treated with ICIs between 2015 and 2024. Cohort 1 included 130 patients in which 15 received ICI rechallenge within the same treatment line following irAE-related interruption and 115 who did not undergo rechallenge. Another 15 patients who underwent ICI rechallenge in a subsequent line of therapy comprised cohort 2. In cohort 1, PFS and DOR did not differ between rechallenged and non-rechallenged patients (HR 1.7, 95% CI 0.31-9.3, p = 0.55; HR 2.7, 95% CI 0.24-31.2, p = 0.42, respectively). Recurrent irAEs occurred in 20%, with recurrence of the same irAE in 7% in cohort 1. In cohort 2, 53% had refractory disease, whereas 47% responded to initial ICI and were subsequently rechallenged at progression. The median PFS was 7.4 months (95% CI: 5.0-NE) and 13.5 months (95% CI 8.1-46.7), respectively. ICI rechallenge after irAE-related interruption was feasible in selected patients.

llm_summary: Immune checkpoint inhibitors are powerful cancer drugs that help the body fight Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, but sometimes they cause serious side effects that force doctors to stop treatment. Researchers studied 145 patients with Hodgkin lymphoma who received these drugs between 2015 and 2024, comparing those who restarted the same drug after experiencing side effects to those who did not restart it. The results showed that patients who restarted the drug had similar survival outcomes and disease control as those who did not restart, and only about one in five patients experienced the same side effects again when rechallenged. These findings suggest that carefully selected patients can safely restart immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment after stopping due to side effects, which could help more patients benefit from these powerful drugs. Future research should continue to identify which patients are safest candidates for restarting these drugs and develop better strategies to manage side effects without losing the cancer-fighting benefits.

llm_summary: Mantle cell lymphoma is a serious type of blood cancer that requires careful treatment planning, and doctors want to know the best way to maintain remission, which means keeping the cancer from coming back after initial treatment. Researchers conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis, which means they gathered and carefully analyzed data from multiple existing studies, to examine whether patients who received bendamustine and rituximab, two chemotherapy drugs given together as a first-line treatment, benefited from continuing rituximab alone as a maintenance therapy to prevent relapse. The study evaluated how often patients stayed cancer-free and how long they survived when rituximab maintenance was added to their initial treatment compared to those who did not receive this additional therapy. The findings from this research help doctors understand whether the extra rituximab treatment after the initial chemotherapy combination improves outcomes for mantle cell lymphoma patients and can guide treatment decisions. This type of analysis is important because it combines evidence from many studies to give doctors clearer answers about which treatment strategies work best for their patients.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Serratus Anterior Plane Block in Pediatric Microtia Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Single-Arm Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Costal cartilage harvest for autologous auricular reconstruction in children with microtia is associated with significant postoperative chest wall pain. Ultrasound-guided serratus anterior plane block (SAPB) has emerged as a promising analgesic technique for this population, yet pooled quantitative estimates of its efficacy and safety are lacking.To perform a systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis estimating the pooled efficacy and safety of ultrasound-guided SAPB in pediatric patients undergoing auricular reconstruction with costal cartilage harvest.We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library from inception to February 26, 2026, following PRISMA guidelines and the Cochrane Handbook. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261293444). Eligible studies enrolled pediatric patients with microtia undergoing auricular reconstruction with costal cartilage harvest and reported at least 1 prespecified outcome. Pooled means and proportions were calculated using the inverse variance method with random-effects models. Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochran Q test and I2 statistic.Five randomized controlled trials enrolling 179 patients were included. Pooled rest pain scores peaked at 12 hours (mean: 3.28, 95% CI: 3.09-3.49; I2=51%) and declined to 1.15 (95% CI: 0.81-1.63) at 48 hours. Cough pain similarly peaked at 12 hours (mean: 4.35, 95% CI: 3.92-4.82; I2=90%) and resolved to mild levels by 48 hours. The pooled mean analgesic duration was 11.65 hours (95% CI: 10.59-12.80; I2=87%), 24-hour PCIA consumption was 55.65 mL (95% CI: 46.13-67.15; I2=99%), and rescue analgesic incidence was 18.37% (95% CI: 11.88%-27.30%; I2=0%). Pooled adverse event rates were low: dizziness 6.10% (95% CI: 3.00%-11.98%), postoperative nausea and vomiting 14.97% (95% CI: 9.96%-21.90%), and pruritus 1.77% (95% CI: 0.51%-5.92%). Pooled mean extubation time was 14.31 minutes (95% CI: 13.66-14.99), and ambulation time was 18.68 hours (95% CI: 17.61-19.83). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the stability of all pooled estimates.Ultrasound-guided SAPB provides consistent early donor-site analgesia in pediatric microtia reconstruction, reducing supplemental opioid requirements and supporting favorable recovery profiles without increasing procedural complications. These findings support its integration into multimodal perioperative analgesia strategies for this population.Level IV-therapeutic study.Copyright © 2026 by Mutaz B. Habal, MD.

llm_summary: Children born with microtia, a condition where the outer ear is underdeveloped, often need surgery to reconstruct their ear using cartilage taken from their ribs, but this procedure causes significant chest wall pain after surgery. Researchers reviewed five clinical trials involving 179 children to evaluate whether a special ultrasound-guided nerve block called a serratus anterior plane block, which numbs the chest area, could safely reduce pain after this type of ear reconstruction surgery. The results showed that this nerve block technique effectively controlled pain for about 11 to 12 hours, with pain levels highest at 12 hours after surgery but dropping to mild levels by 48 hours, while also reducing the need for additional opioid pain medications by about 18 percent. The nerve block had very low rates of side effects, with only about 6 percent of children experiencing dizziness and 15 percent experiencing nausea and vomiting, and children recovered quickly with normal breathing restored in about 14 minutes and ability to walk around within about 19 hours. title: The hepatic sinusoid as a regulatory niche: From cellular specialization to precision hepatology.
abstract: The hepatic sinusoid is increasingly recognized as a multicellular, spatially organized and therapeutically actionable regulatory niche rather than merely a specialized microvascular bed. Liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, hepatic stellate cells, Kupffer cells, recruited leukocytes, lymphocytes, cholangiocytes, hepatocytes and extracellular matrix components form dynamic networks that coordinate vascular exchange, immune surveillance, metabolic zonation, tissue repair and systemic communication. Recent advances in single-cell and spatial omics, quantitative imaging, mechanobiology and human tissue models have revealed how endothelial dedifferentiation, macrophage and T-cell programming, stellate cell plasticity, extracellular matrix remodeling and stromal control of cancer immunity interact across disease stages. These insights recast fibrosis, portal hypertension, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and liver cancer as disorders of sinusoidal communication and niche organization, while linking sinusoidal dysfunction to aging and extrahepatic axes. In this review, we trace the evolution of sinusoidal research from cellular specialization to integrated niche biology, focusing on the next unresolved layer: which cell-cell interactions are causal, how they change with disease stage and how they can be measured or perturbed in human tissue. We define priorities for mapping disease-stage-specific human niches, restoring protective functions, developing composite biomarkers and standardizing translational platforms. The hepatic sinusoid is considered here as a tissue-level regulatory unit whose failure can be interrogated through coupled vascular, stromal, immune, metabolic and mechanical readouts.Copyright © 2026 American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases.

llm_summary: The liver contains a specialized network of blood vessels and cells that work together to control important functions like filtering blood, fighting infection, and managing metabolism, but scientists are now realizing this network is much more complex and important than previously understood. Researchers reviewed recent scientific advances using new technologies like single-cell analysis and imaging that allow scientists to see individual cells and their locations in liver tissue, along with studies using human tissue models to understand how different liver cells communicate with each other. The findings show that when this cellular communication breaks down, it leads to serious liver diseases including scarring, high blood pressure in the liver, fatty liver disease, and liver cancer, and that problems in this network are also connected to aging and diseases in other parts of the body. Understanding which specific cell-to-cell interactions actually cause disease and how these interactions change as disease progresses could lead to new treatments that restore the liver's protective functions and help doctors create better diagnostic tests. The next major challenge for researchers is to map out exactly how these cellular networks function in human patients at different disease stages and to develop standardized methods for testing and treating these problems in human tissue rather than just in laboratory settings.

title: Expert consensus on clinical trials for use of systemic therapy in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma undergoing surgical and locoregional therapies.
abstract: Advances in systemic therapy for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) have fuelled a growing interest in evaluating these therapies in earlier stages of disease. However, trial design remains challenging due to the marked clinical and biological heterogeneity of early-stage and intermediate-stage HCC.A multidisciplinary group of cancer experts was convened by the HCC-Live Consortium to discuss inclusion criteria, risk stratification, treatment arms and appropriate endpoints of trials evaluating perioperative and combination therapies in patients with HCC.Consensus statements were defined as those obtaining >70% approval by panellists.The panel achieved consensus regarding nine consensus statements for neoadjuvant or perioperative systemic therapy and nine statements for combination locoregional plus systemic therapy. Statements emphasised recruiting carefully selected patient populations, employing treatment strategies and duration that balance efficacy with safety and using clinically relevant endpoints. Trials evaluating neoadjuvant/perioperative approaches should include patients at the highest risk of recurrence, with a recommended primary outcome of 2-year event-free survival using restricted mean survival time. Trials evaluating combination therapies should include a homogeneous patient population and use an appropriate comparator arm that aligns with clinical practice. Specifically, systemic therapy was the recommended comparator arm for patients with larger tumour burden and locally advanced disease. The recommended primary outcome for combination trials was progression-free survival and overall survival, with an alpha-recycling strategy. Secondary endpoints are essential to inform clinical applicability.Optimal design of HCC trials is important to rigorously evaluate the role of systemic therapy in patients undergoing surgical resection or in combination with locoregional therapy.© Author(s) (or their employer(s)) 2026. llm_summary: Doctors have developed new cancer drugs that work well for advanced liver cancer, and they want to test whether these drugs can help patients with earlier stages of the disease, but designing these studies is difficult because early liver cancer varies greatly from patient to patient. A large group of cancer experts met together to create guidelines for how to properly design and run these clinical trials, which are research studies that test new treatments on human volunteers. The experts agreed on eighteen key recommendations, including that trials should focus on patients most likely to have cancer return, should measure success using two-year survival rates without cancer growth, and should compare new drug combinations against standard treatments that doctors already use in practice. These guidelines emphasize that researchers need to carefully select which patients participate in trials, choose treatment plans that work well without causing too much harm, and measure outcomes that actually matter to patients in real life. Following these expert recommendations will help doctors and researchers properly test whether combining surgery, local treatments, and systemic drugs (medicines that travel through the whole body) can improve survival and quality of life for people with liver cancer.

title: Risk factors for CRS and ICANS with Bispecific Antibodies for Aggressive Lymphomas.
abstract: Bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) are effective treatments in aggressive B‑cell lymphomas but carry immune-mediated risks of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), particularly during the first cycle. We analyzed 255 patients receiving BsAbs across 14 institutions to identify predictors of CRS/ICANS. CRS occurred in 31% (Grade 3+: 5%) and ICANS in 8% (Grade 3+: 2%) of patients, with no significant differences across glofitamab, mosunetuzumab, or epcoritamab. CRS rates with glofitamab and epcoritamab as monotherapy were lower than reported in trials. In multivariable analysis, concurrent systemic chemotherapy was associated with Grade 2+ CRS, and the development of any-grade CRS and elevated ferritin independently was associated with ICANS. All patients with Grade 3+ CRS had very high serum C-Reactive Protein (sCRP, ≥15 mg/L) and elevated ferritin (>336 ng/mL) when available. These findings identify candidate laboratory thresholds and treatment related factors that warrant prospection validation for risk stratification and outpatient BsAb administration.Copyright © 2026 American Society of Hematology.
